questions.stem: On ticket TICKET-16450 a checker asks which method reliably counts the whole-number points inside a triangular region.

options.text: Multiply the two axis intercepts and halve the result, since every region is a right triangle
options.misconception: treats every region as a right triangle with perpendicular axes

options.text: Fix each value of y in turn, find the whole-number x-values it allows, and add the row counts
Divide the area of the region by the area of one lattice square to get the point count
options.misconception: treats the area as if it equalled the lattice point count

options.text: Count the points on the slanted boundary line and multiply that count by two for the interior
options.misconception: counts only the boundary and doubles the result

questions.explanation: Counting row by row uses the boundary line itself, so every point is counted exactly once and none is missed. The area shortcut fails because the area of a region and the number of its lattice points are different quantities.
questions.hint: Work one row at a time using the boundary line.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Count of whole-number lattice points in a region
questions.learningObjective: verify a claimed lattice-point count in a region
questions.stem: A lattice-check ticket, TICKET-16700, claims the region 3x + 4y ≤ 24 contains 38 whole-number points. Check that claim.

options.text: The region holds 24 points, because the tester counted only the points on the line itself
options.misconception: counts only the boundary points of the region

options.text: The region holds 38 points, because the tester also counted the points on the boundary twice
options.misconception: double counts the boundary points in the total

options.text: The region holds 33 points, because the rows for y = 0 through 6 give 9, 7, 6, 5, 3, 2, 1 points
The region holds 42 points, because the tester used each intercept as a whole row of points
options.misconception: uses the intercepts as if they were whole rows of points

questions.explanation: The rows for y = 0 through 6 give 9, 7, 6, 5, 3, 2, and 1 points, and they sum to 33, so 38 is too many. The tester most likely counted a row the line 3x + 4y = 24 does not allow.
questions.hint: Count each row and add the row totals.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Count of whole-number lattice points in a region
questions.learningObjective: explain a lattice-point count under a single budget line
questions.stem: Ticket TICKET-16950 asks you to explain how many whole-number points lie in the region x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + 3y ≤ 11.

answer.exemplar: Fixing y = 0, 1, 2, 3 and solving x + 3y ≤ 11 for x gives 12, 9, 6, and 3 whole-number x-values, while y = 4 already fails the inequality. Adding 12 + 9 + 6 + 3 gives 30, and each point is counted once because it has exactly one y-value.

questions.explanation: Each whole-number y fixes a row, and the inequality gives 12, 9, 6, and 3 allowed x-values for y = 0 through 3, with no rows beyond that. The sum 12 + 9 + 6 + 3 is 30, and every point is counted once.
questions.hint: Each y-value gives one row of allowed x-values.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Count of whole-number lattice points in a region
questions.learningObjective: apply the row-by-row count to a release budget line
questions.stem: On ticket TICKET-17150 a release region is 2x + 5y ≤ 20 with whole-number x and y at least 0. Apply the row-by-row count and give the number of whole-number points.
questions.explanation: For y = 0 through 4 the allowed x-values number 11, 8, 6, 3, and 1, and y = 5 is already impossible. Those five rows add to 29 whole-number points inside the release region.
questions.hint: For each y, take the largest whole x that fits the line.
